News.title: Age you can legally leave children home alone in England as hundreds of schools shut early due to 40C heat warning
News.content:
WITH hundreds of schools set to close early this week due to extreme heat, children across the country will be gearing up for some unexpected time off.

This could, however, create a dilemma for those parents struggling to arrange last-minute childcare.





In total, 243 schools across England and Wales have announced they will close or finish early for several days this week to protect pupils from extreme temperatures.

A spokesperson from the Department for Education told The Sun: “In terms of who decides if a school stays open or closed, it’s up to the school rather than the local authority.”

Yet when it comes to the rules at home, leaving children on their own is an area fraught not only with moral issues but also legal obligations.

While there is currently no law in England that sets a specific age for leaving a child unsupervised at home, it is a criminal offence if youngsters are put at risk.



Parents can face fines or even jail if a child suffers harm due to being left alone.

Under child protection laws, it is illegal to leave a minor “in a manner likely to cause unnecessary suffering or injury to health”.

Government advice urges parents to use common sense and judge how mature a child is before leaving them on their own, even briefly.

The NSPCC recommends children under the age of 12 are rarely mature enough to be left alone for a long period of time.



Kids aged under 16 should not be left home alone overnight, no matter how responsible they seem.

Babies, toddlers, and very young children must never be left alone, even for a moment.

News.title: The 5 biggest issues facing next Prime Minister from small boats to welfare bill… as Burnham gets his first briefings
News.content:
ANDY Burnham is set to become the next Prime Minister within weeks – and will immediately be confronted with a daunting intray of problems facing the country.

He was only sworn into Parliament on Monday after winning the Makerfield by-election last week.





Burnham’s overwhelming support from Labour MPs triggered Sir Keir Starmer’s resignation and likely “coronation” by July 17.

Downing Street today confirmed that he will start receiving government briefings from the civil service “as soon as possible”.

Sir Keir Starmer has agreed for prospective Labour candidates to meet with the Cabinet Secretary to discuss their plans to ensure a “smooth transition”.

Former Manchester Mayor Burnham had expected to have the summer to prepare his blueprint for government – yet now has a mere month to get ready for the most powerful office in the land.



And so while jubilant Labour MPs rushed to take selfies with their leader-in-waiting, the honeymoon might not last long as he prepares to take on the tough issues.

Here are the five biggest challenges he faces:

Immigration

Controlling immigration is one of the top priorities among voters – both legal net migration and the small boats crisis.

Mr Burnham so far appears to be backing Shabana Mahmood’s reforms to cut the numbers and clamp down on Channel crossings.



In an interview he said immigration must fall further and agreed with the “broad thrust” of the home secretary’s plans.

Ms Mahmood has reformed Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR) which means migrants will have to wait ten years instead of five to claim benefits.

However, more than 11,000 migrants have crossed the Channel in small boats this year and there is a growing appetite among the public to take an even stronger approach to migration.

Defence

Allies of Mr Burnham believe this will be the most difficult department to fund, while Sir Keir’s flagship Defence Investment Plan (DIP) appears to be on ice after his resignation.

Mr Burnham has backed plans by ministers to increase defence spending, but signalled he would be relaxed in borrowing more money to fund the armed forces.



After John Healey’s resignation he said he would reduce the welfare bill to spend more money on defence.

Draft proposals by ministers would only take UK defence spending to 2.86 per cent, well below the ambition of 3 per cent.

It remains unclear what taxes Mr Burnham could increase or what welfare cuts he would be willing to make to pay for this uplift.

Welfare

Attempting to slash the welfare bill shattered Sir Keir’s authority after his own party torpedoed efforts to cut benefits by a mere £6billion.

At the time Mr Burnham joined the rebellion claiming the government had made “the wrong choice”, helping him win over friends on the Left of the party.



But since then Mr Burnham has backtracked after admitting the welfare needed to be cut in a different way.

The welfare bill is expected to soar to £400billion by the end of the decade and is increasingly unaffordable.

Even trimming parts of it will be incredibly unpopular with many of his own MPsand supporters who helped him return to Parliament.

Economy

Mr Burnham inherits an economy plagued by sluggish growth, high taxes and enormous debt.

He will flesh out his plans for the economy next week in a broad pitch on his plans for tax and spending.



Wes Streeting is odds-on to be the next chancellor after dropping out of the leadership contest and throwing his weight behind the former mayor of Manchester.

Mr Streeting’s views on fiscal discipline and honest choices has won him admirers in the City.

But Mr Burnham’s own left-wing platform has sparked fears of a market backlash, especially given his notorious previous remarks that Britain should not be “in hock” to the bond markets.

As Manchester mayor he advocated for stronger public ownership of transport and water and more spending which will cost billions of pounds.

He has vowed to stay within Rachel Reeves’ borrowing rules to avoid racking up debt, and so will have little money to play with.



Brexit

Resetting UK-EU relations was central to part of Sir Keir’s mission as prime minister.

However, his government had strict red lines which ruled out bringing back free movement and rejoining the customs union.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Mr Burnham in the past has said he would like to see the UK rejoin the European Union in the future.

But during the Makerfield by-election campaign he promised not to re-run the Brexit campaign and backtracked on his vision to rejoin the bloc.

Mr Burnham will also be wary that his new constituency strongly voted to leave the EU ten years ago.

News.title: Who should be the next Prime Minister? VOTE NOW
News.content:
POLL OF THE DAY Who should be the next Prime Minister? VOTE NOW

SIR Keir Starmer fought back tears as he announced that he will quit as Prime Minister after less than two years in power.

The PM addressed the nation outside Downing Street yesterday and is set to formally leave No10 by September at the latest.





It remains unclear whether there will be a full-blown leadership battle or whether MPs and unions will quickly unite behind front-runner Andy Burnham – whoever emerges as leader will automatically become PM.

But if the power struggle over No10 went to a general election, then the Conservatives, Reform UK and Restore Britain would campaign hard to gain leadership.

Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, pledges to lower taxes, deregulation, and unshackle the financial sector to boost investment into the UK, saying excessive red tape has killed growth and jobs.

Meanwhile, Reform UK’s Nigel Farage has a strong “stop the boats” policy and pledges to scrap net zero targets to make household bills cheaper, and Rupert Lowe of Restore Britain would bring an even tougher approach to immigration, promising to “deport illegal migrants” if elected.

News.title: Brit man hunted by police after body of model, 36, found inside suitcase by horrified cleaners in rented flat
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

‘MURDER’ RIDDLE Brit man hunted by police after body of model, 36, found inside suitcase by horrified cleaners in rented flat

A MANHUNT has been launched for a British man after the body of a model was discovered stuffed in a suitcase in Colombia.

Cleaning staff found the corpse of model Natalia Villalba Angarita in a rented apartment on the seventh floor of a building in the capital, Bogota.





The 36-year-old was discovered in a large suitcase in the bathroom after staff went to investigate reports of running water.

Personal belongings, including two of her passports – one expired and one valid with stamps showing recent travel to Spain – were recovered from the scene.

Her death is being treated as a possible homicide and violent death.

A British national entered the property on June 17 and left the following day, cops said.



CCTV footage captured the man carrying bed linen to a laundry area.

The video corroborates his presence inside the apartment on June 17.

Investigators says the CCTV has led them to find specific items and locations for potential DNA, fibre and trace evidence recovery.

A US citizen from Texas was also present during the early part of Natalia’s stay in the apartment, according to police.



Security camera recordings, building entry logs and the movements of the two foreign men are now being analysed as part of the investigation.

Forensic experts have sent the body for a post-mortem examination to establish the precise cause and time of death, along with fingerprint and trace evidence.

But both men remain at large and are being actively sought.



No motive has been confirmed and no arrests have been made.

Decades of conflict in Colombia have deepened sexual and gender-based violence that women and girls face.

With 886 recorded femicides in 2024, the country reached a historic seven-year high.

The case has drawn comparisons to the 2023 murder of DJ Valentina Trespalacios, whose body was also found in a suitcase.

In June 2024, a Colombian court found US citizen John Nelson Poulos guilty of aggravated femicide along with concealment and alteration of evidence.



He was sentenced to 42 years and eight months in prison.

News.title: Girl, 2, ‘sexually assaulted and murdered by mum & boyfriend who fractured 21 bones in her body in campaign of abuse’
News.content:
A TODDLER was murdered by her mother and her boyfriend following a harrowing ‘campaign of violence’ in which she sustained 21 broken bones, a court heard.

Isabelle Rose Welsh, two, suffered a catastrophic brain injury having suffered weeks of abuse at the hands of Alexandra Walker and Harrison Simpson, it is alleged.





The youngster endured multiple fractures to 21 bones in the days and weeks before her death on 14 September last year and had also been sexually assaulted, Teesside Crown Court was told.

Walker, 25, and Simpson, 22, deny murder, sexual assault, causing or allowing the death of a child and child cruelty offences.

Opening the case to jurors, Richard Wright, KC, prosecuting, said Isabelle had suffered a ‘campaign of violence’ at her home in Hartington Close, Thornaby, where Simpson was a regular visitor.

The youngster died after allegedly being violently shaken and slammed against a ‘hard, unyielding’ surface on September 13 last year before passing away in hospital in the early hours of the following morning.



Outlining the case, Mr Wright told how paramedics responding to a 999 call discovered Isabelle collapsed at the foot of the stairs covered in bruises, with ‘no pulse and plainly gravely ill’.

He said: ‘Isabelle’s death was not the result of some form of naturally occurring illness.



‘She died because shortly before her terminal collapse somebody had inflicted a massive head injury upon her.

‘Her skull had been fractured, her brain had been injured, and her heart had stopped as a result of that assault upon her.

Mr Wright added: ‘This was no accident. It was the deliberate infliction of injury on that little girl.

”It was, say the prosecution, murder.

‘Neither was the assault on Isabelle an isolated act of violence towards her.’



Post-mortem tests on Isabelle revealed a catalogue of injuries, the jury was told.

She had suffered ‘multiple fractures to no less than 21 bones in her body’, including her arms, legs and spine, and 97 soft-tissue injuries.

The court heard that 11 days before Isabelle died, she was taken by Walker to see a GP who said her daughter was struggling to walk.



Walker reportedly claimed the toddler had trapped her leg in the bars of her cot two weeks earlier. At hospital, an X-ray revealed a spiral fracture of Isabelle’s right shin bone.

Mr Wright said: ‘Her right leg was found to be fractured, but despite the concerns of some of the medical staff, Isabelle was discharged back into the care of her mother, the account of an accidental injury seemingly having been accepted.

‘That earlier fracture to her leg was however no more of an accident than the fatal head injury that killed her.’

Mr Wright said both Walker and Simpson ‘must have been aware’ of the abuse because their two-bedroomed house was ‘so small and the injuries both so severe and obvious’.

He added: ‘For weeks this child had been violently assaulted and her death, by that terrible head injury, was simply the end point in that campaign of violence to which she had been subjected.



‘Who had done this to Isabelle? The prosecution will invite you to conclude that Isabelle had been subjected to that violence by her mother and by her mother’s boyfriend.’

The prosecution alleged that Walker only called 999 on the day of her death after being told to do so by her stepfather ‘long after she must have known her daughter was critically ill.’

Mr Wright said: ‘Their failure to summon help from doctors and finally the emergency services was an act of self-preservation.

‘They knew the questions that would come and had no convincing answer for them.’

The court heard that Simpson and Walker began a relationship in the summer of 2025. Isabelle, born in March 2023, was Walker’s only child.



Mr Wright said: ‘The prosecution say that there is no doubt that this relationship was unhealthy. That it was characterised by drink on the part of Walker and drugs on the part of Simpson.

‘It led to a decline over time in the care that was being given to Isabelle.

‘That then built into her being subjected to regular violence at home by these two defendants.’

Central to the six-week trial is CCTV footage taken from inside Walker’s home.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The court was told that the footage ‘demonstrates the difference’ in Isabelle from June 2025 to the time of her death the following year.



The trial continues.

News.title: I tried ‘World Cup booze-tag’ used to curb violent drunken behaviour…here are ridiculous ways lags have tried to beat it
News.content:
OWN GOAL I tried ‘World Cup booze-tag’ used to curb violent drunken behaviour…here are ridiculous ways lags have tried to beat it

WAKING up with a saliva-starved mouth, stinging headache and a ‘booze tag’ attached to my ankle, I accept my fate… I’m going to jail.

Or at least I would be, if I were a criminal ordered to wear the ‘ankle breathaliser’ – a device which can monitor how much alcohol the wearer has consumed – having flouted the strict no-booze restriction it’s designed to enforce.





Thankfully, in my case, it’s just a test- part of an exclusive demo for the Ministry of Justice’s World Cup violence clampdown from company SCRAM (Secure Continuous Remote Alcohol Monitoring).

A day earlier at 11.15am, I was fitted with the wallet-sized device, used to monitor more than 7,300 destructive drinkers during the World Cup in a bid to curtail boozed-fuelled violence.

The ankle tags, fitted to offenders released from prison on licence or serving community orders, can detect alcohol in as little as 30 minutes after consumption.

Gases emitted through sweat, known as ‘insensible perspiration’, reveal any violations of the no-boozing orders and can lead to further jail time, a court summons or hefty fine.

Alcohol violence is an issue that cost the economy £21 billion last year alone, and the firm claims it has a 97 per cent compliance rate – in addition to many quitting booze after using it.

However that hasn’t stopped many from trying to evade detection. Some have poured alcohol-based gels on it to test a false spike or cut it off – also a violation.

Bizarrely, others have tried to use anything from chicken skin to ham to cheat the tag.

“We’ve seen it all and none of it works,” says Amit Sethi, 45, SCRAM Director of International Operations.



“There have been lots of different things put between the tag’s sensor and the skin to block detection – like a business card, credit card, tin foil – but we can always tell.

“Chicken skin, ham, baloney, condoms and anything that might mimic skin has been tried but it doesn’t work because we can detect the alcohol anyway and any obstructions to readings.

“People wrongly believe if they don’t sweat alcohol won’t be detected. Someone put their foot in a bucket of ice but it didn’t work because your body still emanates the gases.

“In the US, we’ve had people try to shoot the tag off their ankle.

“We’ve seen people try to break it off with force and one person used a nail gun and shot through his own leg.”



They’re all unsuccessful. The device can detect cheating incidents within 30 minutes – which would be flagged as a violation to the Probation Service.

The MoJ believe the SCRAM CAM (Continuous Alcohol Monitoring) tag, which takes 48 readings a day, will reduce the risk of alcohol-related violence for offenders including fights, public disorder and criminality.

Crime data shows 39 per cent of all violent crime and serious offences involve booze and violence against partners spike.

Prisons, Probation and Reducing Reoffending Minister Lord Timpson said he hopes the tech serves as a “wake-up call to offenders” and “sobering thought that one slip-up could send them back to jail”.

He adds: “Major sporting events should be a time for the country to come together and enjoy the game, not for alcohol-fuelled violence and disorder to ruin the occasion.”



The tags are hoped to curb chaos on streets around the country post-England games and avoid the barbarian-like scenes five years ago at the 2020 Euro finals.

Back then, more than 2,000 ticketless yobs stormed Wembley Stadium, bulldozing through safety barriers and assaulting security guards in a reckless bid to watch our loss to Spain on penalties.

Mass brawls erupted, and there were 86 arrests and 19 officers injured on the day of the final.



The booze-detecting tech, known as a “breathaliser for the ankle”, was created by SCRAM Systems’ co-founder Jeff Hawthorne after his best friend from university was killed by a seven-time convicted drink driver.

Since then, they have monitored 1.2 million people – including on Lindsay Lohan, who was ordered to wear the tag in 2008 after a DUI and again in 2010.

Offenders can be ordered to wear the device for between 120 days and one year. If a violation is flagged, data is studied by analysts and then reported to the Probation Service.



Analysts check the reports because other products such as sanitiser gel, aftershave or deodorants – could all trigger a reading.

“We’ve looked into other variables, like food, but you would have to eat 10lb of rum cake in an hour to get a reading. That’s the weight of a newborn baby,” Amit laughs.

“If you drink non-alcoholic beers (normally 0.5%) it won’t work because you can’t consume enough of them in the relevant time period for it to get you intoxicated.

“Your body burns the alcohol too quickly for it to affect you.”

Taking the tag test Sun writer Josh Saunders says: The intention of the demo is to mimic a ‘drinking session’, aka binge drinking, like a person might do during a World Cup match to test the speed of detection and my alcohol data. Tightly fitted to my leg, the tag gently vibrates with a text alert ‘buzz’ as it establishes my body temperature, alcohol consumption rate – currently zero – and other measures. It takes 12 readings over the first hour and then one every half hour. Once ready, I down a shot – a 40 per cent ABV, double whiskey (two alcohol units) – and I quickly feel the effects. The tech detects alcohol through the gases from sweat. At 1.41pm, I glug part of a pint of four per cent Shepherd Neame Creekside Juicy IPA (2.3 units). Six minutes later, the first reading of alcohol is detected by the tag. In a real scenario, this reading would have been flagged to the Probation Service. At this point, I’m told of a previous ankle-tag ‘guinea pig’ with a low alcohol tolerance who had to be put home in a taxi with a McDonald’s by now. Next up, at 2.02pm, a double Gordon’s gin and tonic (two units), which has an ABV of 37.5 per cent. 10 minutes later I bump into the table heading to the bathroom. The tag feels uncomfortable but I’m beginning to forget it’s there. I walk outside with it on show and get a couple of sniggers from passersby. After one final drink, a four per cent Whitstable Bay IPA (2.3 units) at 2.56pm, I leave, now rather drunk. Sweat begins to pour from my body. Around 52 minutes later (3.48pm), I’m at my peak alcohol level – my Transdermal Alcohol Concentration (TAC) is 0.237. This means I’m roughly four times over the drink-drive limit thanks to eight units of booze. It took until 8.24pm – five hours after my “high-level drinking session” ended – to be below the drink-drive limit. I’m told my body is quick to process alcohol, for others it could be longer before they are legally able to drive. The typical rate is one hour per unit of alcohol. It makes me fear for fellow England fans embarking on a similarly boozy binges to mine. If they finish drinking post-midnight, as could happen due to later World Cup finish times, they could be over the drink-drive limit when driving to work. The ankle tag is being lauded by the Government and Police Crime Commissioners as a brilliant initiative. I can see why. There is no clear way to cheat the device and it’s backed by ‘tried, tested and proven’ science. Plus the device will reportedly save the taxpayer money. It costs approximately £60,000 to hold a person in prison per year, but with this tech, fitted to offenders released on licence or in community orders, the cost is “thousands of pounds”. For the 7,300 offenders wearing the SCRAM tag through the World Cup – their term of monitoring typically ranges between 120 days and a year. 97 per cent of offenders on the tag comply with the rules. Many hope tags for illegal drugs will be developed in the future. The success rate and savings are sobering thoughts in the battle against booze-related harm – even for someone nursing a hangover, like me.



Dorset Police Crime Commissioner (PCC) David Sidwick, 64, tells us they “really, really welcome” the ankle tag’s use to curb “lairy behaviour”.

“Virtually every police force in the country has a plan around how to police the World Cup,” the APCC Joint Lead on Addictions and Substance Misuse says.

“It’s part of the package to incentivise offenders not to commit crime and to rehabilitate.

“If it helps violent individuals give up alcohol too, that’s a good thing.

“It’s the few who need to be addressed, not the millions of fans having a good time watching games.”



Booze-tag violations are easily detectable and the data, combined with analysis by the SCRAM team, is used in court – leaving Amit to share a clear, sobering message.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“If you have drunk alcohol while wearing the device, there is no activity – whether that’s exercise, drinking coffee, vomiting, or blocking the sensor – that you can do to stop it being detected.

“Once the alcohol is in your body, our bodies are very efficient at processing it out of the system. So we will know and you will be caught.”

News.title: We asked Sun readers if there should be a snap general election and who should be PM – and your response was deafening
News.content:
YOUR SAY We asked Sun readers if there should be a snap general election and who should be PM – and your response was deafening

SIR Keir Starmer announced he will quit as Prime Minister after less than two years in power.

The PM fought back tears as he resigned outside Downing Street yesterday morning with his likely replacement Andy Burnham arriving in London just hours later.





The former Manchester mayor was sworn in as an MP and if he remains unchallenged for the Labour Leadership, he could be Prime Minister by July 17 so we asked you, what should happen now? Should there be an election?

Thousands of you reacted, and an 19,000 of you said YES the public should have their say.

Only 1,000 of our readers said no while 2,000 were unsure.

We also asked who you think should be the next PM – to which dozens of you said Reform’s Nigel Farage would make the best leader.



While a small number of you said an election could unleash more chaos, and that Mr Burnham had the potential to be a good PM.

WHAT DO YOU THINK? HAVE YOUR SAY HERE

One reader said: “There should be an immediate GE when a new Labour PM is elected.

“The new elected Labour PM should go to the country for any approval of any of their policies.”



Many others agreed and another said: “I strongly believe the general public have every right to vote who they want as next PM and therefore a general election pronto please.”

One added that Sir Keir deserved better, they wrote: “I think Starmer was a great prime minister he deserved more time to prove himself. He didn’t deserve to be stabbed in the back by labour MPs.”

Others stated they were glad to see the back of him: “At last the worst ever PM has resigned. Lets have a general election now so that the public have a say in who the next PM is.”

A reader said that in his time as PM: “Starmer has destroyed our country, economy and standing in the world. He is worst PM and leader ever as is this Labour government.

“He’s done nothing to stop immigration and protect woman and children from these mainly young men pouring unchecked into our country. Welfare, national debt, unemployment have risen by staggering amounts.”



One said that Mr Burnham will only add fuel to the fire as PM: “There should be a general election, we should have a say on who leads our country,

“It’s looking like Andy Burnham will get it and god help us if he does, because we are all going to hell in a handcart.”

Another said: “Burnham was not even an MP before by election. He only represents the gentrified people of Manchester (and Liverpool) a lot like the London labour MPs.”

However, one reader commented: “I think Andy Burnham appears to be a good potential PM but I fear that the Starmer allies will cause problems and demand a leadership election.

“I think there will be more chaos if there is a general election. I have never supported Labour but everything is in such a mess that change needs to happen now. Defence must be sorted now.



“A general election will cause more problems and cost the country a fortune.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But most of you agreed that “too many times we have been landed with a prime minister we haven’t voted for from parties that never seem to put the country first.”
